Forecasting COE Supply 8-12 Quarters Ahead

DBA3702 group project: predictive-modelling workflow in R

DBA3702 Group Project

Data: LTA, Jan 2010 to Oct 2026

Problem statement. Can COE supply be forecast far enough ahead, and with honest uncertainty, for a dealer or fleet operator to price and time real financial exposure?

How the analysis is built.

Step What we do
Forecast contract Use only information published up to the forecast month
Target Monthly car deregistrations (Cat A + B), 1-36 months ahead
Baseline quota.sg-style: rolling 12-month average carried forward
Evidence for the approach Fig 02: correlation with COEs won k months earlier (the 10-year lag)
Features Hypotheses H1-H8 turned into feature groups
Leakage test Change the future; the features must not change
Validation Rolling-origin backtest (expanding window)
Models Rolling average, linear regression (cohort), Ridge, random forest
Selection rule Simpler model unless the leader is better by > 2 SE and a practical threshold
Feature-group ablation Remove each group in turn from the full linear model
Prediction intervals Empirical forecast-error ratios by horizon
Uncertainty of the gain Moving-block bootstrap; fan chart from whole error paths
Held-out test Last 24 months of targets kept out of model selection
Decision outputs 12-quarter quota fan chart and order-book exposure by timing shift

0. Settings: everything the group may want to change is here

What this section does. Every choice the group might change (horizon, validation/test split, practical threshold, simulation count, example order book) lives here, so the whole analysis can be rerun with one edit. Two choices matter most: the 36-month horizon matches the 8-12 quarter planning window dealers and fleet operators need (quota.sg stops at 3 quarters), and the Aug 2024 split keeps the last 24 months completely out of model selection.

DATA_DIR   <- "data"
OUT_DIR    <- "outputs"
H_MAX      <- 36            # forecast horizon in months (12 quarters)
CV_START   <- "2019-01"     # first forecast origin in the backtest
VAL_END    <- "2024-08"     # targets up to here = validation; after = test (frozen)
PRACTICAL  <- 0.02          # a gain must be >= 2% of mean monthly deregs to count
COVID_CB   <- c("2020-04", "2020-05", "2020-06")   # bidding suspended
SEED       <- 3702
N_SIM      <- 2000          # simulated paths for the fan chart
PATH_FROM  <- "2020-07"     # error paths for the fan: origins after the 2020 suspension
                            # (earlier origins had < 4.5 years of training data)
C_RECENT_Q <- 4             # recent quarters used to sample LTA's "Part c" (one draw per path)
# Aug-Oct 2026 has only 5 of 6 exercises in the data; use LTA's announced quota
# (news release 24 Jul 2026: Cat A 7,134 + Cat B 5,527)
ANNOUNCED_AB <- c("2026-08" = 7134 + 5527)
ORDER_BOOK <- c(50, 50, 50, 50)   # cars the dealer must register in the next 4 quarters
dir.create(OUT_DIR, showWarnings = FALSE)
set.seed(SEED)

# Month index helpers: integer months make "10 years earlier" exact arithmetic
mi      <- function(ym) as.integer(substr(ym, 1, 4)) * 12L + as.integer(substr(ym, 6, 7)) - 1L
mi_ym   <- function(i) sprintf("%d-%02d", i %/% 12L, i %% 12L + 1L)
mi_date <- function(i) as.Date(paste0(mi_ym(i), "-01"))
find_file <- function(name) {
  f <- list.files(DATA_DIR, pattern = name, recursive = TRUE, full.names = TRUE)
  if (length(f) == 0) stop("Put ", name, " in ", DATA_DIR)
  f[1]
}
save_plot <- function(p, file, w = 10, h = 5) {
  ggsave(file.path(OUT_DIR, file), p, width = w, height = h, dpi = 150, bg = "white")
  print(p)                                       # show the figure in the notebook
}

1. Question and objective

  • Decision supported: a dealer pricing a forward order book, or a fleet planning a replacement cycle, wants to know whether COE supply in each of the next 12 quarters will be high or low, and how sure we can be.
  • Prediction task: at the end of month o (the origin), forecast car deregistrations (Cat A + B) for months o+1 … o+36, then turn them into quota using LTA’s formula (25% of the last 12 months’ deregistrations, plus adjustments “Part c”).
  • Forecast contract: only information published up to month o.
  • Success: (1) lower error than the quota.sg-style rolling average, at every horizon. and (2) prediction intervals whose stated coverage holds on the frozen test.
  • Out of scope: forecasting premiums (they also depend on demand). Section 9 only shows the supply-driven part of premium risk.

2. Inspection and cleaning

What this section does. Loads the five LTA files, fixes known format problems and builds the three series the model uses: monthly car deregistrations (Cat A + B, the thing we forecast), monthly PQP (the renewal price) and the number of cars in each age band (the cohort pipeline).

Why it matters. Two traps are handled here rather than inside the model: bid counts stored as text with commas (“1,232”), and the oldest age band spelled two ways (“20 and above” / “20 & above”). Each file also ends in a different month, so everything is cut at the last month common to deregistrations and ages.

results <- read_csv(find_file("M11-coe_results.csv"), col_types = cols(.default = "c")) %>%
  mutate(across(c(quota, bids_success, bids_received, premium), parse_number),  # "1,232" -> 1232
         bidding_no = as.integer(bidding_no), t = mi(month))
pqp     <- read_csv(find_file("M11-coe_results_pqp.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) %>% mutate(t = mi(month))
dereg   <- read_csv(find_file("M05-Dereg_by_Quota.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) %>% mutate(t = mi(month))
reval   <- read_csv(find_file("M10-Monthly_COE_Revalidation.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) %>% mutate(t = mi(month))
age     <- read_csv(find_file("M01-03M-Age.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  mutate(t = mi(month),
         band = as.integer(parse_number(age)))   # "9 - < 10" -> 9; "20 and above" / "20 & above" -> 20

cat("\n== 2.1 Coverage ==\n")

for (nm in c("results", "pqp", "dereg", "reval", "age")) {
  d <- get(nm)
  cat(sprintf("%-8s %s to %s, %d rows\n", nm, mi_ym(min(d$t)), mi_ym(max(d$t)), nrow(d)))
}

# Monthly series used throughout
y_tbl <- dereg %>% filter(category %in% c("Category A", "Category B")) %>%
  group_by(t) %>% summarise(y = sum(number), .groups = "drop")       # car deregs, A + B
pqp_tbl <- pqp %>% filter(vehicle_class %in% c("Category A", "Category B")) %>%
  group_by(t) %>% summarise(pqp = mean(pqp), .groups = "drop")
cars <- age %>% filter(type == "Cars") %>% select(t, band, number)
stopifnot(all(count(cars, t)$n == 21), !anyNA(cars$number))          # 21 bands, no gaps for cars

T_LAST <- min(max(y_tbl$t), max(cars$t))                             # common end: Aug 2026
cat("Modelling data end (common to dereg and age):", mi_ym(T_LAST), "\n")
Modelling data end (common to dereg and age): 2026-08

Observations (2).

  • The five files cover 2010-2026 for prices, 2014-2026 for deregistrations and 2016-2026 for ages. The binding constraint is the age data, which starts in January 2016, so the model can learn from about ten years.
  • Bidding was suspended in April-June 2020. These months are kept, with a flag (cb), because a business must plan for shocks too.
  • All files are cut at August 2026, the last month present in both the deregistration and age data. Bidding results run to October 2026, but using them would mix information the model cannot have at the same time.
# Stock matrix: rows = months, columns = age bands 0..20
S_mat <- cars %>% pivot_wider(names_from = band, values_from = number) %>% arrange(t)
T0 <- min(S_mat$t)
S_mat <- as.matrix(S_mat[, as.character(0:20)])
stock <- function(tt, b, S = S_mat) S[cbind(tt - T0 + 1L, b + 1L)]

3. Visualisation (EDA)

What this section does. Three charts test the project’s central claim before any model is built: is COE supply mechanical (decided years in advance by who registered when), and does the renewal price change it?

# Fig 01 - the cohort wave: cars by age band over time
p01 <- cars %>% mutate(date = mi_date(t)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(date, band, fill = number / 1000)) + geom_raster() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Cars ('000)") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 9.5, colour = "white", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "Fig 01. Car population by age band - the large 2016-2018 cohorts approach year 10",
       subtitle = "Dashed line = the 10-year COE expiry. Diagonals are cohorts ageing one band per year.",
       x = NULL, y = "Age band (years)") + theme_minimal()
save_plot(p01, "fig01_cohort_wave.png")

Observations (Fig 01).

  • Each diagonal is a registration cohort ageing one band per year. The bright band now sitting at ages 7-10 holds about 239,000 cars (77.7k, 83.7k and 77.3k in the three bands), against only about 19,000 cars aged 10-11.
  • These are the large 2016-2018 cohorts. They reach their 10-year decision (renew or scrap) between 2026 and 2029, which is the supply wave the forecast must capture.
  • Ages 2-4 are thin (about 27-38k per band), reflecting the tight quotas of 2022-23, so a supply trough should follow around 2032-34.
  • Why it matters: most of the next three years’ supply is already parked on the road, visible in public data today. A fleet planning a replacement cycle is choosing between landing in this wave or in the trough after it.
# Fig 02 - which past month best predicts today's deregistrations?
reg_tbl <- results %>% filter(vehicle_class %in% c("Category A", "Category B")) %>%
  group_by(t) %>% summarise(reg = sum(bids_success), .groups = "drop")   # registrations proxy
lag_corr <- map_dfr(seq(96, 132, 1), function(k) {
  d <- y_tbl %>% inner_join(reg_tbl %>% mutate(t = t + k), by = "t")
  tibble(months_back = k, correlation = cor(d$y, d$reg), pairs = nrow(d))
})
p02 <- ggplot(lag_corr, aes(months_back, correlation, fill = months_back %% 12 == 0)) +
  geom_col() + scale_fill_manual(values = c("steelblue", "salmon"), guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "Fig 02. Correlation of car deregistrations with COEs won k months earlier",
       subtitle = "Red = whole years. Supply is mechanical: today's scrapping was decided by registrations ~10 years ago.",
       x = "Months back", y = "Correlation") + theme_minimal()
save_plot(p02, "fig02_lag_correlation.png")

cat("\n== 3. Strongest lag:", lag_corr$months_back[which.max(lag_corr$correlation)],
    "months, r =", round(max(lag_corr$correlation), 3), "\n")

== 3. Strongest lag: 120 months, r = 0.877

Observations (Fig 02).

  • Car deregistrations correlate most strongly with COEs won exactly 120 months earlier (r = 0.88), the 10-year COE life. A year either side (108 or 132 months) the correlation falls to about 0.6.
  • Why it matters: this is the evidence that supply is substantially mechanical. A rolling average of recent deregistrations (quota.sg’s method) ignores this signal; a cohort model uses it directly.
# Fig 03 - the feedback loop: renewal rate vs PQP (rolling 12 months)
renew_tbl <- reval %>% filter(category %in% c("Category A", "Category B")) %>%
  group_by(t) %>% summarise(renewals = sum(number), .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(t) %>%
  mutate(renew12 = stats::filter(renewals, rep(1, 12), sides = 1)) %>%  # trailing 12-month sum
  filter(t - 12 >= T0, t <= max(cars$t)) %>%
  mutate(due12 = stock(t - 12, 9),               # cars that were 9-10 a year ago = reached 10 since
         renew_rate = as.numeric(renew12) / due12) %>%
  left_join(pqp_tbl, by = "t") %>% filter(!is.na(renew_rate))
p03 <- ggplot(renew_tbl, aes(pqp / 1000, renew_rate, colour = mi_date(t))) +
  geom_point() + geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, colour = "black", formula = y ~ x) +
  scale_colour_date(name = NULL) + scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) +
  labs(title = "Fig 03. Renewal rate vs Prevailing Quota Premium (A + B, trailing 12 months)",
       subtitle = "Approximate: renewals / cars that reached year 10 (includes year-15 and year-20 renewals).",
       x = "PQP (S$ '000)", y = "Renewals per car reaching 10") + theme_minimal()
save_plot(p03, "fig03_feedback.png")

cat("Correlation renewal rate vs PQP:", round(cor(renew_tbl$renew_rate, renew_tbl$pqp), 3), "\n")
Correlation renewal rate vs PQP: -0.349

Observations (Fig 03).

  • Taken on its own, the renewal rate is lower when PQP is high (r = -0.35), the opposite of the simple feedback story.
  • This raw chart is confounded by time. The denominator (cars reaching year 10) grew sharply from 2024 as the big 2016-18 cohorts arrived, while PQP rose over the same years. Renewals did rise in absolute terms (26,770 in 2024 to 32,783 in 2025), but not as fast as the cohort.
  • The model in sections 6-7 separates the two effects. Holding cohort size fixed, higher PQP does mean fewer year-10 cars are scrapped (the negative due10 x lpqp coefficient in section 7).
  • Why it matters: a raw scatter would mislead an audience. The feedback loop exists, but it only shows once the cohort wave is accounted for.

4. Hypotheses -> feature groups

# Hypothesis Evidence Becomes
H1 Cars reaching year 10 drive deregistrations Fig 01, 02 due10
H2 Cars on 5-year renewals must leave at year 15 Revalidation data due15
H3 Cars on 10-year renewals decide again at year 20 Revalidation data due20
H4 High PQP makes owners renew instead of scrapping Fig 03 lpqp, due10 x lpqp
H5 Deregistrations have a calendar pattern - month of year
H6 Recent level carries extra information - recent12
H7 Nonlinear effects beyond these - random forest
H8 Many coefficients may overfit - Ridge

5. Features - built only from data up to the origin month o

What this section does. Turns the age table into forecast inputs. For any forecast month and horizon (1-36 months ahead), it counts the cars that will reach year 10, 15 or 20 in that month, using only data available at the forecast date. It adds the PQP at that date, the recent 12-month level, the calendar month and the 2020 flag.

Why it matters. A forecast that accidentally uses future information looks excellent in a backtest and fails in real use. The leakage test below triples every number after the forecast date and checks that no feature changes; the script stops if one does.

A car in age band b at month o reaches age b + 1 within the next 12 months. So cars due at year 10 in months o + 1 … o + 12 sit in band 9 at o; for o + 13 … o + 24 they sit in band 8 (and must survive one more year), and so on. Survival between bands is estimated only from age snapshots seen by o.

survival_at <- function(o, S = S_mat) {
  # one-year survival ratio band b -> b+1, using pairs (t, t+12) with t+12 <= o
  if (o - 12L < T0) return(rep(1, 20))           # first year: no pairs yet, assume no losses
  ts <- T0:(o - 12L)
  sapply(0:19, function(b) min(1, mean(S[ts + 12L - T0 + 1L, b + 2L] / S[ts - T0 + 1L, b + 1L])))
}

build_features <- function(o, h = 1:H_MAX, S = S_mat, y = y_tbl, pq = pqp_tbl) {
  sv <- survival_at(o, S)
  k  <- (h - 1L) %/% 12L                         # whole years ahead
  surv_to <- function(from, to) sapply(from, function(f) if (f > to) 1 else prod(sv[(f:to) + 1L]))
  b10 <- 9L - k; b15 <- 14L - k; b20 <- 19L - k
  tibble(
    origin = o, h = h, t = o + h,
    due10  = stock(o, b10, S) * surv_to(b10, 8L) / 12,
    due15  = stock(o, b15, S) * surv_to(b15, 13L) / 12,
    due20  = stock(o, b20, S) * surv_to(b20, 18L) / 12,
    lpqp   = log(pq$pqp[pq$t == o] / 50000),     # centred at S$50k
    recent12 = mean(y$y[y$t > o - 12L & y$t <= o]),
    moy    = factor((o + h) %% 12L + 1L, levels = 1:12),
    cb     = as.integer(mi_ym(o + h) %in% COVID_CB)   # calendar fact, known in advance
  )
}

# Leakage test: changing anything after the
# origin must not change the features.
o_test <- mi("2022-06")
f1 <- build_features(o_test)
S_fake <- S_mat; future_rows <- which((T0:(T0 + nrow(S_mat) - 1L)) > o_test); S_fake[future_rows, ] <- S_fake[future_rows, ] * 3
y_fake <- y_tbl %>% mutate(y = if_else(t > o_test, y * 3, y))
p_fake <- pqp_tbl %>% mutate(pqp = if_else(t > o_test, pqp * 3, pqp))
f2 <- build_features(o_test, S = S_fake, y = y_fake, pq = p_fake)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(f1, f2)))
cat("\n== 5. Leakage test passed: features ignore everything after the origin ==\n")

== 5. Leakage test passed: features ignore everything after the origin ==
# Panel of (origin, horizon) rows, every origin with stock and 12 months of history
panel <- map_dfr(max(T0, min(y_tbl$t) + 11L):(T_LAST - 1L), build_features) %>%
  left_join(y_tbl, by = "t")                     # y is NA beyond T_LAST
cat("Panel rows:", nrow(panel), "| with known target:", sum(!is.na(panel$y)), "\n")
Panel rows: 4572 | with known target: 3942

Observations (5).

  • The leakage test passes: features depend only on information available at the forecast date.
  • The panel has 4,572 (forecast date x horizon) rows, 3,942 of which have a known outcome to learn from or score against.

6. Modelling

What this section does. Competes seven models on equal terms, from the quota.sg-style rolling average up to a random forest. Every model is refitted at each forecast date from January 2019 using only data up to that date, then forecasts the next 36 months. This rolling-origin backtest is the honest way to score a time-series forecast, because it reproduces how the tool would have performed if used live.

Why it matters. The business claim is “we forecast further ahead and better than the existing tool”. This section is where that claim is tested, with a selection rule fixed before looking at the test period.

FORMULAS <- list(
  cohort   = y ~ due10 + due15 + due20,
  feedback = y ~ due10 + due15 + due20 + lpqp + due10:lpqp,
  full     = y ~ due10 + due15 + due20 + lpqp + due10:lpqp + moy + recent12 + cb,
  # lean = groups the ablation in 6.3 found helpful (set after the ablation)
  lean     = y ~ due10 + lpqp + due10:lpqp + moy + cb
)
MODELS <- tibble(
  model      = c("Rolling average (quota.sg-style)", "Linear | cohort", "Linear | cohort + feedback",
                 "Linear | lean", "Linear | full", "Ridge | full", "Random forest | full"),
  complexity = c(0, 1, 2, 2.5, 3, 4, 5)
)

fit_predict <- function(train, test, which = MODELS$model) {
  out <- tibble(.rows = nrow(test))
  if ("Rolling average (quota.sg-style)" %in% which) out[["Rolling average (quota.sg-style)"]] <- test$recent12
  if ("Linear | cohort" %in% which) out[["Linear | cohort"]] <- predict(lm(FORMULAS$cohort, train), test)
  if ("Linear | cohort + feedback" %in% which) out[["Linear | cohort + feedback"]] <- predict(lm(FORMULAS$feedback, train), test)
  if ("Linear | lean" %in% which) out[["Linear | lean"]] <- predict(lm(FORMULAS$lean, train), test)
  if ("Linear | full" %in% which) out[["Linear | full"]] <- predict(lm(FORMULAS$full, train), test)
  if ("Ridge | full" %in% which) {
    X  <- model.matrix(FORMULAS$full, train)[, -1]
    Xt <- model.matrix(update(FORMULAS$full, NULL ~ .), test)[, -1]
    cv <- cv.glmnet(X, train$y, alpha = 0, nfolds = 5)
    out[["Ridge | full"]] <- as.numeric(predict(cv, Xt, s = "lambda.1se"))
  }
  if ("Random forest | full" %in% which) {
    rf <- ranger(y ~ due10 + due15 + due20 + lpqp + moy + recent12 + cb, data = train,
                 num.trees = 300, min.node.size = 20, seed = SEED)
    out[["Random forest | full"]] <- predict(rf, test)$predictions
  }
  # deregistrations cannot be negative or collapse to nothing: floor at 20% of the recent level
  out %>% mutate(across(everything(), ~ pmax(.x, 0.2 * test$recent12)))
}

6.1 Rolling-origin backtest (expanding window)

For origin o: train on rows whose target month <= o, predict o+1..o+36.

run_backtest <- function(formulas_override = NULL, which = MODELS$model, origins = mi(CV_START):(T_LAST - 1L)) {
  if (!is.null(formulas_override)) { old <- FORMULAS; FORMULAS <<- formulas_override; on.exit(FORMULAS <<- old) }
  suppressWarnings(map_dfr(origins, function(o) {   # early origins: rank-deficient fits warn
    train <- panel %>% filter(t <= o, !is.na(y))
    test  <- panel %>% filter(origin == o, !is.na(y))
    if (nrow(test) == 0) return(NULL)
    bind_cols(test %>% select(origin, h, t, y), fit_predict(train, test, which)) %>%
      pivot_longer(-c(origin, h, t, y), names_to = "model", values_to = "pred")
  }))
}
cat("\n== 6.1 Running rolling-origin backtest ... ==\n")

== 6.1 Running rolling-origin backtest ... ==
bt <- run_backtest() %>%
  mutate(window = if_else(t <= mi(VAL_END), "validation", "test"),
         hq = ceiling(h / 3), horizon = cut(hq, c(0, 4, 8, 12), labels = c("Q1-4", "Q5-8", "Q9-12")),
         err = pred - y, abs_err = abs(err))

hourly_like <- bt %>% filter(window == "validation") %>%
  group_by(model, horizon) %>% summarise(MAE = mean(abs_err), .groups = "drop") %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = horizon, values_from = MAE) %>%
  left_join(bt %>% filter(window == "validation") %>% group_by(model) %>%
              summarise(MAE_all = mean(abs_err), bias = mean(err)), by = "model") %>%
  left_join(MODELS, by = "model") %>% arrange(MAE_all)
cat("\nValidation MAE (cars per month), by horizon:\n"); print(hourly_like, width = 200)

  <chr>                             <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>  <dbl>      <dbl>
1 Linear | lean                      578.   759.    961.    735.  301.         2.5

Observations (6.1). Validation error (cars per month; lower is better):

  • Every cohort-based linear model beats the quota.sg-style rolling average at every horizon. At 9-12 quarters ahead the rolling average misses by 1,829 cars a month; the cohort model misses by 859, less than half.
  • The rolling average’s error grows steadily with horizon, and it is biased low by about 1,055 cars a month: carrying the recent level forward misses the cohort wave that is coming.
  • The flexible models do not win. The full linear model (1,031) and the random forest (1,169) are worse than the 3-variable cohort model (748). With about ten years of monthly data, extra flexibility mostly fits noise.

6.2 Selection rule

rank by pooled validation MAE; prefer the simpler model unless the leader beats it by > 2 SE (paired by origin) AND >= PRACTICAL.

paired_gain <- function(a, b, win = "validation", d = bt) {
  # positive = model a has lower error than model b
  x <- d %>% filter(window == win, model %in% c(a, b)) %>%
    group_by(origin, model) %>% summarise(mae = mean(abs_err), .groups = "drop") %>%
    pivot_wider(names_from = model, values_from = mae) %>% na.omit()
  g <- x[[b]] - x[[a]]
  tibble(a = a, b = b, mean_gain = mean(g), se = sd(g) / sqrt(length(g)),
         origins_better = sum(g > 0), origins = length(g))
}
threshold <- PRACTICAL * mean(y_tbl$y[y_tbl$t <= mi(VAL_END)])
leader <- hourly_like$model[1]
sel_tbl <- map_dfr(setdiff(MODELS$model, leader), ~ paired_gain(leader, .x)) %>%
  mutate(clearly_better = mean_gain > 2 * se & mean_gain >= threshold)
cat(sprintf("\nLeader: %s. Practical threshold: %.0f cars/month\n", leader, threshold))

Leader: Linear | lean. Practical threshold: 88 cars/month
print(sel_tbl, width = 200)

not_beaten <- c(leader, sel_tbl$b[!sel_tbl$clearly_better])
SELECTED <- MODELS %>% filter(model %in% not_beaten) %>% arrange(complexity) %>% slice(1) %>% pull(model)
cat("SELECTED:", SELECTED, "\n")
SELECTED: Linear | cohort

Observations (6.2).

  • Linear | lean has the lowest validation error, but it beats the simpler Linear | cohort by only 10 cars a month (SE 47), far below the 88-car practical threshold.
  • Under the rule, the simplest model the leader does not clearly beat is chosen: Linear | cohort, which uses only cars reaching years 10, 15 and 20.
  • Why it matters: the chosen model is easy to explain on one slide (“count the cars coming due”), which builds trust with a dealer audience.
p04 <- bt %>% filter(window == "validation") %>% group_by(model, hq) %>%
  summarise(MAE = mean(abs_err), .groups = "drop") %>%
  ggplot(aes(hq, MAE, colour = model)) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) + geom_point() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:12) +
  labs(title = "Fig 04. Validation error by forecast horizon",
       subtitle = "Rolling origins 2019 onward; targets up to Aug 2024. Lower is better.",
       x = "Quarters ahead", y = "MAE (car deregistrations per month)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
save_plot(p04, "fig04_mae_by_horizon.png")

Observations (Fig 04). The gap between the rolling average (top line) and the cohort models widens with horizon. That is exactly the 8-12 quarter window where dealers and fleets lack tools today, and where our approach adds the most.

6.3 Feature-group ablation on the full linear model

What this section does. Removes each feature group in turn from the full linear model and measures how much the error changes. A group whose removal makes the forecast better is not earning its place.

cat("\n== 6.3 Ablation: remove one group at a time from Linear | full ==\n")

== 6.3 Ablation: remove one group at a time from Linear | full ==
full_terms <- c("due10", "due15", "due20", "lpqp", "due10:lpqp", "moy", "recent12", "cb")
groups <- list("year-10 cohort (H1)" = "due10", "year-15 expiries (H2)" = "due15",
               "year-20 decisions (H3)" = "due20", "PQP feedback (H4)" = c("lpqp", "due10:lpqp"),
               "month of year (H5)" = "moy", "recent level (H6)" = "recent12")
abl <- map_dfr(names(groups), function(g) {
  keep <- setdiff(full_terms, groups[[g]])
  if (g == "year-10 cohort (H1)") keep <- setdiff(keep, "due10:lpqp")
  f <- reformulate(keep, "y")
  b <- run_backtest(modifyList(FORMULAS, list(full = f)), which = "Linear | full") %>%
    mutate(window = if_else(t <= mi(VAL_END), "validation", "test"), abs_err = abs(pred - y),
           model = "without")
  both <- bind_rows(bt %>% filter(model == "Linear | full") %>% select(origin, h, t, window, model, abs_err),
                    b %>% select(origin, h, t, window, model, abs_err))
  paired_gain("Linear | full", "without", d = both) %>% transmute(removed = g, MAE_increase_when_removed = mean_gain, se)
})
print(abl, width = 200)
# A tibble: 6 x 3
  removed                MAE_increase_when_removed    se
  <chr>                                      <dbl> <dbl>
1 year-10 cohort (H1)                       241.   63.9 
2 year-15 expiries (H2)                    -183.   71.8 
3 year-20 decisions (H3)                     40.7  55.0 
4 PQP feedback (H4)                          -7.75  7.03
5 month of year (H5)                         20.3  19.7 
6 recent level (H6)                         -82.2  13.4

Observations (6.3).

  • Cars reaching year 10 is essential: removing it adds 241 cars a month of error.
  • Year-15 expiries and the recent level hurt the full model (removing them cuts error by 183 and 82). Recent level double-counts what the cohort already says, and the age band 14-15 mixes 5-year renewers (who must leave) with 10-year renewers (who stay), so it is a noisy signal.
  • PQP feedback adds nothing detectable for forecasting (-8, SE 7), even though section 7 shows the effect is real. The feedback changes which year-10 cars leave, but its size is small next to the size of the cohort.
  • The groups that helped were kept as the lean set (year-10 cohort, PQP feedback, month of year, 2020 flag), which then competed in 6.2.

7. Diagnostics and what the model learned

What this section does. Fits the full model on all data to read what it has learned, and checks whether the chosen model is systematically too high or too low in any year.

cat("Reading: due10 = share of cars reaching year 10 that are scrapped in that month;",
    "a negative due10:lpqp means higher PQP -> fewer of them scrapped (the feedback loop).\n")
Reading: due10 = share of cars reaching year 10 that are scrapped in that month; a negative due10:lpqp means higher PQP -> fewer of them scrapped (the feedback loop).

Observations (7).

  • due10 = 0.64: at a PQP of S$50,000 (where lpqp = 0), about 64 of every 100 cars reaching year 10 are deregistered. At today’s PQP of about S$120,000 the model puts it nearer 53, because of the feedback term below.
  • The feedback loop is real: the due10 x lpqp term is negative and highly significant (t = -6.7). At today’s cohort sizes, a 10% rise in PQP means roughly 35 fewer deregistrations a month, and therefore less future quota.
  • The 2020 suspension cut deregistrations by about 840 cars a month while it lasted.
  • Bias by year: the chosen model under-forecast 2020-21 (COVID) and over-forecast 2019 and 2022, but is within about 100-200 cars a month in 2023-24. Errors are largest around the pandemic, which is why the fan chart in 9.1 drops paths that start before July 2020.

8.1 Prediction intervals

empirical error ratios by horizon year (calibrated on validation), coverage checked on test - the COE version of “calibration”.

ratios <- bt %>% filter(model == SELECTED) %>% mutate(ratio = y / pred, year_ahead = (h - 1) %/% 12 + 1)
bands <- ratios %>% filter(window == "validation") %>% group_by(year_ahead) %>%
  summarise(lo80 = quantile(ratio, .10), hi80 = quantile(ratio, .90),
            lo95 = quantile(ratio, .025), hi95 = quantile(ratio, .975), .groups = "drop")
coverage <- ratios %>% filter(window == "test") %>% left_join(bands, by = "year_ahead") %>%
  group_by(year_ahead) %>% summarise(covered80 = mean(ratio >= lo80 & ratio <= hi80),
                                     covered95 = mean(ratio >= lo95 & ratio <= hi95), n = n())
cat("\n8.1 Interval multipliers (validation) and coverage on test:\n"); print(bands); print(coverage)

Observations (8.1). The intervals come from the ratio of actual to forecast in validation, separately for 1, 2 and 3 years ahead.

  • The bands widen with horizon (80% range of about +/-29% one year ahead, wider beyond), which is the honest shape for a fan chart.
  • On the test they are conservative: the 80% band contained 91-99% of outcomes. Validation included the COVID period, which inflates the bands.
  • Why it matters: for a dealer, a band that is slightly too wide is safer than one that is too narrow. Report this openly as a calibration finding, as the proposal promised.

8.2 How certain is the gain over the rolling average

Moving-block bootstrap over consecutive origins (origins overlap, so they are not independent).

block_boot <- function(a, b, win = "test", block = 6, B = 2000) {
  x <- bt %>% filter(window == win, model %in% c(a, b)) %>%
    group_by(origin, model) %>% summarise(mae = mean(abs_err), .groups = "drop") %>%
    pivot_wider(names_from = model, values_from = mae) %>% na.omit() %>% arrange(origin)
  n <- nrow(x); starts <- 1:(n - block + 1)
  gains <- replicate(B, {
    idx <- unlist(lapply(sample(starts, ceiling(n / block), replace = TRUE), function(s) s:(s + block - 1)))[1:n]
    1 - mean(x[[a]][idx]) / mean(x[[b]][idx])
  })
  tibble(a = a, vs = b, block = block, gain_pct = 100 * (1 - mean(x[[a]]) / mean(x[[b]])),
         lo95 = 100 * quantile(gains, .025), hi95 = 100 * quantile(gains, .975))
}
cat("\n8.2 Error reduction vs rolling average, test, moving-block bootstrap:\n")

8.2 Error reduction vs rolling average, test, moving-block bootstrap:
print(map_dfr(c(3, 6, 12), ~ block_boot(SELECTED, "Rolling average (quota.sg-style)", block = .x)))

3 Linear | cohort Rolling average (quota.sg-style)    12     39.1  23.4  55.0

Observations (8.2). Consecutive forecast dates overlap, so they are resampled in blocks.

  • The chosen model reduces error by 39% against the quota.sg-style method (95% interval 23-55%), and the interval stays well above zero for 3, 6 and 12-month blocks.
  • Why it matters: this is the headline competitive claim, and it is statistically secure, not a lucky period.

       x = NULL, y = "Car deregistrations per month (A + B)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")

Observations (Fig 05).

  • Forecasts made in August 2021, 2023 and 2024 are compared with what happened (grey). The cohort model anticipates the 2025-26 rise in deregistrations (the forecast made in August 2024 overshoots it, as more owners renewed than in the past); the rolling average stays flat and misses the rise entirely.
  • The cohort forecast moves in yearly steps because age bands are one year wide. A future improvement is to use monthly registrations (from bidding results) to give a smoother monthly shape.

9. Communication and decision

What this section does. Turns the validated model into the three outputs the business needs: a deregistration forecast with uncertainty, a quota projection for the next 12 quarters, and the COE cost of a dealer’s order book under different purchase timings.

9.1 Final forecast from the latest origin, with simulated paths

Each path re-uses a whole historical error path (all 36 horizons from one origin), so errors stay correlated across horizons - a bootstrap over origins.

o_now <- T_LAST
train_all <- panel %>% filter(!is.na(y))
f_now <- build_features(o_now)
f_now$pred <- fit_predict(train_all, f_now, SELECTED)[[SELECTED]]
path_matrix <- function(from) {
  ratios %>% filter(origin >= mi(from)) %>% group_by(origin) %>% filter(n() == H_MAX) %>% ungroup() %>%
    select(origin, h, ratio) %>% pivot_wider(names_from = h, values_from = ratio) %>%
    select(as.character(1:H_MAX)) %>% as.matrix()
}
R <- path_matrix(PATH_FROM)
R_all <- path_matrix(CV_START)                       # sensitivity: every origin, incl. 2019-20
cat(sprintf("\n== 9.1 Forecast from %s using %d complete historical error paths ==\n", mi_ym(o_now), nrow(R)))

== 9.1 Forecast from 2026-08 using 38 complete historical error paths ==
sim_from <- function(Rm) Rm[sample(nrow(Rm), N_SIM, replace = TRUE), ] * matrix(f_now$pred, N_SIM, H_MAX, byrow = TRUE)
sim_y <- sim_from(R)

fan_m <- tibble(t = f_now$t, central = f_now$pred,
                lo80 = apply(sim_y, 2, quantile, .10), hi80 = apply(sim_y, 2, quantile, .90),
                lo95 = apply(sim_y, 2, quantile, .025), hi95 = apply(sim_y, 2, quantile, .975))
p06 <- ggplot(fan_m, aes(mi_date(t))) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo95, ymax = hi95), fill = "steelblue", alpha = .2) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo80, ymax = hi80), fill = "steelblue", alpha = .35) +
  geom_line(aes(y = central), colour = "steelblue4", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_line(data = y_tbl %>% filter(t >= mi("2019-01")), aes(mi_date(t), y), colour = "grey30") +
  labs(title = "Fig 06. Car deregistrations (A + B): history and 36-month forecast",
       subtitle = paste0("Model: ", SELECTED, ". Bands: 80% and 95% from bootstrapped historical error paths."),
       x = NULL, y = "Deregistrations per month") + theme_minimal()
save_plot(p06, "fig06_dereg_fan.png")

Observations (Fig 06).

  • The model expects about 6,000 car deregistrations a month, roughly 72,000 a year through 2027-28, up from about 62,000 over the last 12 months, as the 2016-2018 cohorts reach year 10.
  • The 80% band is built from 38 complete historical error paths. Reusing whole paths keeps a bad year bad, so the band reflects realistic runs of over- or under-forecasting, not independent monthly noise.

9.2 From deregistrations to quota

Quota for the quarter starting qs = c * 25% * deregistrations over months qs-13 .. qs-2 (LTA’s formula, Part a) where c captures Part c (injections, cut-and-fill, expired TCOEs, Cat E share).

quota_hist <- results %>% filter(vehicle_class %in% c("Category A", "Category B")) %>%
  mutate(qs = t - ((t %% 12L) - 1L) %% 3L) %>%           # quarter starts: Feb, May, Aug, Nov
  group_by(qs) %>% summarise(quota = sum(quota), exercises = n_distinct(paste(t, bidding_no)), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(quota = if_else(mi_ym(qs) %in% names(ANNOUNCED_AB), unname(ANNOUNCED_AB[mi_ym(qs)]), quota),
         exercises = if_else(mi_ym(qs) %in% names(ANNOUNCED_AB), 6L, exercises)) %>%
  filter(exercises == 6)                               # complete quarters only (drops 2020 suspension)
window_sum <- function(qs, yv) sapply(qs, function(q) { w <- yv[as.character((q - 13L):(q - 2L))]; if (anyNA(w)) NA else sum(w) })
y_named <- setNames(y_tbl$y, y_tbl$t)
quota_hist <- quota_hist %>% mutate(formula = 0.25 * window_sum(qs, y_named), c = quota / formula) %>% filter(!is.na(c))
cat("\n9.2 LTA Part c ratio (quota / formula), every complete quarter:\n")

Observations (Part c). The ratio of actual quota to LTA’s formula (25% of the last 12 months’ deregistrations) shows LTA’s own adjustments:

  • 2016-2019: about 0.85-0.95, below 1 because part of the replacement COEs goes to Cat E.
  • Late 2023-2025: 1.2-1.4, the 20,000-COE injection plus early release of guaranteed deregistrations.
  • Since late 2025 it has fallen fast, to 0.84 in Aug-Oct 2026. This is consistent with injections tapering and earlier releases being netted off.
  • Why it matters: Part c is the least predictable part of supply because it is policy. The projection therefore samples it from the last four quarters, and the “formula only” line shows the result without any top-ups.
c_pool <- tail(quota_hist$c, C_RECENT_Q)

future_qs <- seq(mi("2026-11"), by = 3L, length.out = 12)
sim_quota <- function(c_mode = c("recent", "formula"), sims = sim_y) {
  c_mode <- match.arg(c_mode)
  sapply(seq_len(N_SIM), function(s) {
    yv <- c(y_named, setNames(sims[s, ], f_now$t))
    cc <- if (c_mode == "recent") sample(c_pool, 1) else 1     # one policy regime per path
    cc * 0.25 * window_sum(future_qs, yv)
  })   # rows = quarters, cols = simulations
}
QS <- sim_quota("recent"); QF <- sim_quota("formula"); QA <- sim_quota("recent", sim_from(R_all))
fan_q <- tibble(qs = future_qs, quarter = mi_ym(future_qs),
                median = apply(QS, 1, median), lo80 = apply(QS, 1, quantile, .10), hi80 = apply(QS, 1, quantile, .90),
                formula_only = apply(QF, 1, median),
                hi80_all_origins = apply(QA, 1, quantile, .90))   # sensitivity
cat("\nProjected A + B quota per quarter (quarter = first month):\n"); print(fan_q %>% mutate(across(where(is.double), round)))

Observations (Fig 07). This is the headline chart for the deck.

  • Combined Cat A + B quota is projected to rise from about 12,700 a quarter now to about 15,500 for Nov 2026 - Jan 2027, then to 16,000-17,500 a quarter through 2029.
  • The 80% range widens from about 13,300-17,700 next quarter to about 12,000-22,700 by 2028. The lower end barely moves; the uncertainty is mostly on the upside.
  • The red crosses (formula only, no top-ups) sit slightly above the median, because LTA’s recent adjustments have been below 1.
  • Live check: LTA announces the Nov 2026 - Jan 2027 quota this month. Comparing it with the 13,300-17,700 range is a genuine out-of-sample test to present.
  • Why it matters: this is the supply view dealers and fleets cannot get today: 12 quarters ahead, as a range. Because it is combined A + B, it remains valid if LTA merges the two categories.

9.3 Exposure (illustrative)

supply-driven part of premium risk only. Elasticity of premium to quota from quarter-on-quarter changes.

prem_q <- results %>% filter(vehicle_class %in% c("Category A", "Category B")) %>%
  mutate(qs = t - ((t %% 12L) - 1L) %% 3L) %>% group_by(qs) %>%
  summarise(premium = mean(premium), .groups = "drop") %>% inner_join(quota_hist, by = "qs") %>%
  arrange(qs) %>% mutate(dlp = log(premium) - lag(log(premium)), dlq = log(quota) - lag(log(quota)))
el <- lm(dlp ~ dlq, prem_q)
beta <- coef(el)["dlq"]; beta_se <- summary(el)$coefficients["dlq", "Std. Error"]
cat(sprintf("\n9.3 Premium elasticity to quota: %.2f (SE %.2f), R2 %.2f. Demand is NOT modelled.\n",
            beta, beta_se, summary(el)$r.squared))

9.3 Premium elasticity to quota: -0.29 (SE 0.11), R2 0.14. Demand is NOT modelled.

Observations (9.3). This step is deliberately labelled illustrative.

  • Quarter-on-quarter, a 1% rise in quota goes with a 0.29% fall in premium (SE 0.11), but quota explains only 14% of premium movements. Demand, credit and policy drive the rest, which is why the project forecasts supply, not premiums.
prem_now  <- results %>% filter(t == max(t), vehicle_class %in% c("Category A", "Category B")) %>% summarise(mean(premium)) %>% pull()
quota_now <- tail(quota_hist$quota, 1)                # latest complete quarter (Aug-Oct 2026)
betas <- rnorm(N_SIM, beta, beta_se)
prem_paths <- sapply(seq_len(N_SIM), function(s) prem_now * (QS[, s] / quota_now)^betas[s])   # quarters x sims
exposure <- map_dfr(0:2, function(shift) {
  cost <- colSums(prem_paths[(1:4) + shift, , drop = FALSE] * ORDER_BOOK)
  tibble(shift_quarters = shift, expected = mean(cost), p10 = quantile(cost, .1), p90 = quantile(cost, .9))
})
cat(sprintf("Order book: %s cars over 4 quarters, current premium S$%s\n", sum(ORDER_BOOK), comma(prem_now)))
Order book: 200 cars over 4 quarters, current premium S$130,050
print(exposure %>% mutate(across(-shift_quarters, ~ comma(round(.x, -3)))))
# A tibble: 3 x 4
  shift_quarters expected   p10        p90       
           <int> <chr>      <chr>      <chr>     
1              0 24,052,000 22,494,000 25,418,000
2              1 23,872,000 22,111,000 25,448,000
3              2 23,848,000 21,826,000 25,628,000
write_csv(exposure, file.path(OUT_DIR, "exposure_by_shift.csv"))

p08 <- ggplot(exposure, aes(factor(shift_quarters), expected / 1e6)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue", width = .6) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = p10 / 1e6, ymax = p90 / 1e6), width = .2) +
  labs(title = "Fig 08. COE cost of the order book if purchases are shifted (supply-driven part only)",
       subtitle = "Bars = expected cost, whiskers = 10th-90th percentile. Premium also depends on demand, which this does not model.",
       x = "Shift (quarters later)", y = "COE cost (S$ million)") + theme_minimal()
save_plot(p08, "fig08_exposure_shift.png")

Observations (Fig 08).

  • For a dealer registering 200 cars over the next four quarters at today’s premium (S$130,050), the supply-driven expected COE cost is about S$24.1 million, with an 80% range of S$22.5-25.4 million.
  • Shifting purchases one or two quarters later lowers the expected cost by only about S$0.2 million (under 1%), while widening the range.
  • Why it matters: the uncertainty (about S$3 million between the 10th and 90th percentiles) is about 15 times larger than anything timing saves. For a dealer guaranteeing package prices, pricing in the risk band matters more than trying to time the market. That is the case for a tool that shows the distribution, not a point estimate.
cat("\nDone. Figures and CSVs in", OUT_DIR, "\n")

Done. Figures and CSVs in outputs

10. Summary for the report

Business question. Can COE supply be forecast far enough ahead, and with honest uncertainty, for a dealer or fleet operator to price and time real financial exposure?

Answer: yes, for supply.

  1. Supply is substantially mechanical. Car deregistrations track COEs won exactly 10 years earlier (r = 0.88), and about 239,000 cars aged 7-10 will reach their 10-year decision between 2026 and 2029.
  2. A simple cohort model beats the existing approach. Counting the cars coming due cuts forecast error by 39% (95% interval 23-55%) compared with the rolling average quota.sg uses. The gain is largest 2-3 years ahead, the horizon businesses plan on.
  3. The forecast comes with an honest range. Cat A + B quota is projected at about 15,500 next quarter and 16,000-17,500 a quarter through 2029, with an 80% range of roughly 12,000-22,700 by 2028. The ranges proved conservative on held-out data.
  4. The renewal feedback loop is real but small. Higher PQP means fewer year-10 cars are scrapped, holding cohort size fixed, but it does not improve forecasts at current cohort sizes.
  5. For a dealer, risk outweighs timing. On a 200-car order book, delaying purchases saves under 1%, while the uncertainty range spans about S$3 million.

Limitations to state openly.

  • Age data are by vehicle type, so Cat A and Cat B are modelled together. That also makes the projection robust to the proposed A/B merger.
  • LTA’s own adjustments (Part c) are policy, not mechanics; they are sampled from recent quarters, and they have fallen from about 1.3 to 0.84 within a year.
  • Validation includes the COVID period, which makes the intervals conservative.
  • Premiums are not forecast; the exposure step shows only the supply-driven part.

Next steps. Compare the Nov 2026 - Jan 2027 announcement with the projected range; test the lean model further, since it was best on the test period; and add monthly registrations so forecasts move smoothly within each year.
